title: WITAWITADD - Yo Dawg, I Heard You Like Games
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nRTuARH-N9A

Prompted by picking up Call to Adventure, Daniel (@dungeondive) sketches out a sub-genre he thinks deserves a name: games you play *before* other games. Not filler while you wait for the fourth player — games with a utilitarian purpose, designed or repurposed to make the session that follows richer.

Microscope is the headline example, used at his table for pre-game worldbuilding and currently run alongside an in-progress D&D campaign to flesh out the setting as they go. Its virtue is putting everyone on the same page about the world before play starts. Fiasco does the same job for relationships rather than geography. The Quiet Year is a deck of playing cards with the suits split into seasons and a communal map you draw together, answering prompts — a great atrocity is revealed, who uncovers it? — and it would set up Mutant Year Zero beautifully. Elsewhere he pulls tools out of games he doesn't even like: the art cards from Story Master's Tales, drawn at random, become character-generation prompts. Dixit and a stark black-and-white deck called Shindig Machine serve as divination at the D&D table: what would my character do? Life and Legend gets a sympathetic hearing as a strange, almost spiritual life-journey game let down by a rulebook that explains its rules but never its intent. And Dungeon Crusade ships with a whole overworld board game in the box.

The pattern he notices: nearly all of them run on a deck of cards.

----

What do you use to get into your character's head before a campaign starts — a dedicated worldbuilding game, a repurposed card deck, or nothing at all?
